claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature loading.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature loading.
Severe lattice distortion is responsible for the alloy's enhanced plastic strain and toughness.
Severe lattice distortion creates a distributed network of nanoscale obstacles.
The nanoscale obstacle network includes controlled precipitates and/or phase heterogeneities.
The nanoscale obstacles interact with dislocations.
The lattice-distortion-derived network facilitates distributed dislocation motion and dynamic recovery.
Distributed dislocation motion and dynamic recovery enhance plasticity.
The obstacle network delays crack initiation and propagation.
Delayed crack initiation and propagation improve toughness.
Under matched high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit higher strain at failure than pure tungsten.
Under matched high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater resistance to crack growth than pure tungsten.
The proposed behavior is limited to high-temperature, strain-rate, and environmental conditions relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field specifies an arc-melted and thermomechanically processed alloy versus commercially pure tungsten in their respective as-processed states, whereas the conditions and experiment require identical sample preparation or processing. These descriptions do not establish a genuinely identical processing history.

The mediator permits precipitates and/or phase heterogeneities, but the falsification rule treats absence of nanoscale precipitate effects as sufficient to falsify the mechanism. Absence of precipitates would not exclude the alternative obstacle types allowed by the stated mediator.
